page.text_excerpt: Jim Calabro About RSS | Atom | JSON --- Bluesky GitHub Chess Last.fm One Hash Bloom Filters Oct 17, 2026 Note: as always, all my public writing is written by hand by me. Overview A bloom filter is a probabilistic data structure that allows you to quickly and cheaply answer the question "is key X in this set?" with either "definitely not" or "probably". You pick a false positive rate that is acceptable for your workload and hardware, add keys to the set, and check for their existence later on. Bloom filters use a small amount of memory compared to the cardinality of the set, and are computationally very cheap. For these reasons, they're frequently used in high performance data systems. For example, a database might keep an in-memory bloom filter and check it before actually going to disk when looking up rows. This saves substantial amounts of very slow disk IO. We also use them all over the place in the Bluesky backend. They allow us to save millions of queries per second against our Scylla database when looking up blocks, mutes, labels, and more. For instance, we can often answer the question "does user X block user Y" without even hitting the database. Here's the last several days of some of our bloom filter positive hit rates: The above yellow line has a roughly 1% positive rate, which means that 99% of the time, we can completely skip querying our database. This has been critical in our ability to scale the site and operate the site cheaply. Traditional Bloom Filters A bloom filter is an array of bits and k hash functions. You choose the size of the array and k before hand, and want to right-size it to your workload to achieve a specific false positive rate. To add a key to the set, run it through the k hash functions and set the bits at each of those locations. page.text_excerpt: Skip to main content Sign Up Log In ​ ​ Let’s Encrypt is adding two additional remote perspectives for domain validation API Announcements post by Phil 5 days ago Phil Let's Encrypt staff 1 5d Hey everybody, Let's Encrypt is adding two new remote perspectives for domain validation. This change is motivated by the fact that increased perspectives provide more domain validation security and is required by the Baseline Requirements which is quoted below. Increasing the number and coverage of our domain validation perspectives improves visibility and protection against BGP attacks. BR 3.2.2.9 Multi Perspective Issuance Corroboration Effective 2026-12-15, the CA MUST implement Multi-Perspective Issuance Corroboration using at least five (5) remote Network Perspectives. The CA MUST ensure that the requirements defined in Quorum Requirements Table are satisfied, and the remote Network Perspectives that corroborate the Primary Network Perspective fall within the service regions of at least two (2) distinct Regional Internet Registries. If the requirements are not satisfied, then the CA MUST NOT proceed with issuance of the Certificate. During domain validation, this means that we will make seven total validation requests, one from the primary datacenter and six from remote perspectives (previously four). For validation to succeed, the primary server and a quorum of remote perspectives must receive the correct challenge response. This makes it more difficult for attackers to hijack validation requests. To learn more about multi-perspective domain validation, please see our earlier blog post when Let's Encrypt first added new perspectives. We expect little to no impact to users. Let's Encrypt will begin performing domain validation with the new regions in staging on Tuesday, October 27th, 2026. page.title: Rapid alternation of conscious and suppressed stimulus representations in the primate brain
page.description:
The neural correlates of consciousness remain elusive [1]. Previous studies found that high-level visual cortex is weakly modulated by conscious perception [2,3], yet a pure signal of conscious perception has not been found anywhere in the brain. Here, we employed Neuropixels recordings across multiple face patches in inferotemporal and prefrontal cortex during a binocular flash suppression paradigm [4], in which one of two images is consciously perceived while the other, though continuously present, is suppressed from awareness. We found that, during a constant stimulus and percept, the brain rapidly alternates, about 15 times per second, between conscious and suppressed micro-epochs. During conscious micro-epochs, a pure signal of conscious perception was present, allowing accurate reconstruction of the conscious image from neural activity. During suppressed micro-epochs this reversed: the pure signal now tracked the suppressed stimulus, allowing accurate reconstruction of the suppressed image. At the single-cell level, neurons responded selectively to the conscious stimulus and not to the suppressed stimulus during conscious micro-epochs; conversely, during suppressed micro-epochs, neurons responded selectively to the suppressed stimulus. Despite this apparent symmetry, the two epochs could be reliably distinguished, with feature tuning amplified during conscious micro-epochs. Recordings in prefrontal cortex yielded qualitatively similar results. Together, these findings show that both inferotemporal and prefrontal cortex rapidly interleave conscious with suppressed content, indicating that conscious access requires temporal selection beyond localization.

page.description: CSS can now handle tooltip and dropdown positioning without JavaScript. Learn how anchor positioning, popovers, and anchor-size() simplify UI.
page.text_excerpt: Skip to main content Matt Smith About Elsewhere MODERN WEB ENGINEERING, FRONT-END FIRST CSS does your tooltip positioning now 3 min read 2,409 views If you’ve ever built a tooltip, a footnote, or a popover then you’ve written some version of this: const rect = trigger.getBoundingClientRect(); tooltip.style.top = `${rect.bottom + 8}px`; tooltip.style.left = `${rect.left}px`; Looks fine, right? Until the window resizes. Or until the page scrolls. Or the tooltip happens to land near the bottom of the viewport and renders half off-screen because nothing told it to flip to the other side. Not too great. So you add a resize listener, then a scroll listener. Then some manual math to detect overflow and flip the positioning, or you find a JS library to own the math. CSS can do all of this now. No JavaScript, no library, no listeners involved. The core trick: anchor-name and position-anchor Give the element you want to position relative to an anchor-name: .term { anchor-name: --my-anchor; } Then tell the thing that should follow it to use that anchor: .note { position: fixed; position-anchor: --my-anchor; position-area: bottom; } Anchor positioning only works on elements that are already absolutely or fixed positioned. The browser keeps recalculating that position as the page scrolls or resizes. The Trolley Problem, briefly The Trolley Problem is a famous thought experiment in ethics. First posed by Philippa Foot in 1967 and named by Judith Jarvis Thomson, the most well-known formulation asks a simple question: If a train is barreling down the tracks toward five people, and you are at a switch that would divert the train and cause it to kill only one person, would you? Should you? Decide to act, and you save several lives. But your action also means you chose to end a particular life. It’s a tough question, and a classic for a reason. Tonight, I’m looking back through the photo album from my three years at Apple in Cupertino.

So if you ever meet someone who tells you, “At Apple, I’m the one who did this,” take it with a grain of salt. They were probably part of the team that made it happen, and that’s already something to be proud of. 

Sometimes, when the final product finally comes out, you can recognize a few of the personal touches you contributed along the way. And that, in itself, is immensely rewarding.

They can support a range of activities from writing code and researching products to analyzing revenue, processing expenses, and acting across the systems that run the business. To be most useful, they often need access to company data, applications, tools, and other agents. That access is what makes agents more capable. With that capability can come insider risk. This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised. Their models can produce variable outputs, their context can change, and their plans can evolve as they work. An agent that operates as intended when a task begins may respond differently as context or inputs change. Depending on how they are designed and deployed, agents can operate continuously, at machine speed and scale. The gist: American Airlines CEO Robert Isom appeared in court yesterday as part of the current Department of Justice case. While being questioned, the topic of JetBlue Mint came up, which is JetBlue’s business class product. Isom claimed that he has never flown JetBlue Mint, and doesn’t know if JetBlue Mint is lie-flat. He then clarified that he understands that Mint is JetBlue’s domestic first class, but “can’t speak to all the amenities they include.” Here’s the part that I’ve been thinking about: I’ve had the opportunity to interact with quite a few senior airline executives over the years, and I find that their knowledge about competitors is typically one extreme or the other: Some airline executives literally couldn’t tell you the first thing about their competitors, and have no knowledge of their passenger experience, fleet, etc. Some airline executives know literally everything about their competitors, down to being able to tell you how many seats competitors have on specific planes I find there are very few executives who are just kind of in the middle, as it’s pretty polarizing. Without naming any names, I’ll say that generally speaking there’s a high correlation between airlines that have a great passenger experience, and airlines that have executives that keep very close tabs on the competition.
